'''unreproachableness''' (un-rē-prō′cha̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unreproachable; irreproachableness.

'''unreproachably''' (un-rē-prō′cha̤-bli), ''adv.'' Irreproachably.

'''unreprovable''' (un-rẹ̄-prö′va̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unreprovable''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''reprovable.''] Not reprovable; not deserving reproof; without reproach; not liable to be justly censured. Also spelled ''unreproveable.''
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unreprovable'' unto my wyfhood ay.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Good Women, l. 691.}}}}
{{smaller block|My presumption of coming in print in this kind hath hitherto been ''unreprovable.''
{{right|''Ford'', Lover’s Melancholy, Ded.}}}}

'''unreproved''' (un-rẹ̄-prövd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not reproved; not censured.
{{smaller block|Christians have their churches, and ''unreproved'' exercise of religion. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes.}}}}
'''2.''' Not liable to reproof or blame.
{{smaller block|<poem>The gentlewoman has been ever held
Of ''unreproved'' name.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, iv. 2.}}
<poem>Mirth, admit me of thy crew,
To live with her and live with thee
In ''unreproved'' pleasures free.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', L’Allegro, l. 40.}}}}
'''3†.''' Not disproved.
{{smaller block|The ''unreproved'' witnesse of those men’s actions.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', III. 684. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''unrepulsable''' (un-rẹ̄-pul′sa̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being repulsed. ''Jane Austen'', Mansfield Park, xxxiii.

'''unreputable''' (un-rep′ụ̄-ta̤-bl), ''a.'' Not reputable; disreputable.
{{smaller block|Piety is no ''unreputable'' qualification.
{{right|''J. Rogers.''}}}}

'''unrequested''' (un-rẹ̄-kwes′ted), ''a.'' Not requested; not asked.
{{smaller block|<poem>An ''unrequested'' star did gently slide
Before the wise men to a greater light.</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, iv. 2.}}}}

'''unrequisite†''' (un-rek′wi-zit), ''a.'' Not requisite or necessary; unnecessary. ''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, iii. § 11.

'''unrequitable''' (un-rẹ̄-kwī′ta̤-bl), ''a.'' Not requitable; not capable of being requited, recompensed, repaid, or the like. ''Boyle'', Works, I. 274.

'''unrequited''' (un-rẹ̄-kwī′ted), ''a.'' Not requited; not recompensed; not reciprocated.
{{smaller block|It is thought a disgrace to love ''unrequited.'' But the great will see that true love cannot be ''unrequited.''
{{right|''Emerson'', Essays, 1st ser., p. 198.}}}}

{{right|''R. Broughton'', Not Wisely, but Too Well, vi.}}}}

'''unresisting''' (un-rē-zis′ting), ''a.'' Not making resistance; not opposing; submissive; humble. ''Dryden'', tr. of Ovid’s Pythagorean Philosophy.

'''unresistingly''' (un-rẹ̄-zis′ting-li), ''adv.'' In an unresisting manner; without resistance; submissively.

'''unresolvable''' (un-rẹ̄-zol′va̤-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being resolved, in any sense. ''South'', Sermons, V. ix.

'''unresolve''' (un-rē-zolv′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''resolve.''] To give up or change a resolution. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|<poem>Tost by contrary thoughts, the man
Resolv’d and ''unresolv’d'' again.</poem>
{{right|''Ward'', England’s Reformation, iv. 387. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unresolved''' (un-rē-zolvd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not resolved; not determined. ''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 4. 436.—'''2.''' Not solved; not cleared: as, doubt ''unresolved.'' ''Locke.''—'''3.''' Not separated, to the eye or other sense, into its constituent parts: as, an ''unresolved'' nebula; also, not reduced to a state of solution.

'''unresolvedness''' (un-rẹ̄-zol′ved-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unresolved or undetermined; irresolution; indecision.

{{smaller block|Many grow old in an ''unresolvedness'' whether to embrace Christianity or not; and many continue unresolved as long as they live. {{right|''J. Edwards'', Works, IV. 339.}}}}

'''unresolving''' (un-rē-zol′ving), ''a.'' Not resolving; undetermined. ''Dryden.''

'''unrespect†''' (un-rē-spekt′), ''n.'' Disrespect; want of respect or reverence; disesteem. ''Bp. Hall.''
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''unrespectable''' (un-rẹ̄-spek′ta-bl), ''a.'' Not respectable; disreputable; dishonorable.

{{smaller block|He makes no distinction of respectable and ''unrespectable.'' {{right|''H. Bushnell'', Sermons for the New Life, p. 341.}}}}

'''unrespective†''' (un-rẹ̄-spek′tiv), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not regarding circumstances or conditions; devoid of respect or consideration; regardless; unthinking.

{{smaller block|<poem>I will converse with iron-witted fools
And ''unrespective'' boys; none are for me
That look unto me with considerate eyes.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 2. 29.}}
<poem>O too, too rude hand
Of ''unrespective'' death!</poem>
{{right|''Marston'', Antonio and Mellida, II., iv. 3.}}}}

'''2.''' Not respected; used at random; unheeded; common.

{{smaller block|<poem>Nor the remainder viands
We do not throw in ''unrespective'' sieve,
Because we now are full.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 2. 71.}}}}

'''unrespited''' (un-res′pi-ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not respited. —'''2†.''' Admitting no pause or intermission. ''Milton'', P. L., ii. 185.

'''unresponsal†''' (un-rẹ̄-spon′sa̤l), ''a.'' Irresponsible.

{{smaller block|A tithe or a crop of hay or corn which are ready to be carried away by force by ''unresponsal'' men. {{right|''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, p. 106. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unresponsible''' (un-rẹ̄-spon′si-bl), ''a.'' Irresponsible.

{{smaller block|His ''unresponsable'' memory can make us no satisfaction. {{right|''Fuller'', Worthies, Essex, i. 370. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unresponsibleness''' (un-rẹ̄-spon′si-bl-nes), ''n.'' Irresponsibility. ''Bp. Gauden'', Hieraspistes,
readings.c3s2:
p. 349.

'''unresponsive''' (un-rẹ̄-spon′siv), ''a.'' Not responsive.

'''unresponsiveness''' (un-rẹ̄-spon′siv-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unresponsive.

'''unrest''' (un-rest′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unreste'' (= MLG. ''unreste, unraste'' = G. dial. ''unrast''); < ''un-'' + ''rest''<sup>1</sup>.] Lack of rest or quietude, physical or mental.
{{smaller block|“Is this,” quod she, “the cause of youre ''unreste?''”
{{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 248.}}
<poem>That ''unrest'' which men miscall delight
Can touch him not and torture not again.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Adonais, xl.}}}}

'''unrest†''' (un-rest′), ''v. t.'' [ME. ''unresten''; < ''unrest'', ''n.''] To disturb; deprive of rest.
{{smaller block|<poem>Goode is hem to slee,
For thai the swarme ''unresteth'', so thai crie.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 155.}}}}

'''unrestful''' (un-rest′fůl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not restful or at rest; restless. ''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 961.—'''2.''' Not affording rest or promotive of rest.

'''unrestfulness''' (un-rest′fůl-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unrestful; restlessness; disquietude.
{{smaller block|Whiche put the said Vortiger to great ''unrestfulnesse.''
{{right|''Fabyan'', Chronicle, lxxxii. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''unresting''' (un-res′ting), ''a.'' Not resting; continually in motion or action; restless. ''Daniel'', Civil Wars, i.
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''unrestingly''' (un-res′ting-li), ''adv.'' In an unresting manner; continuously; without rest.

'''unrestingness''' (un-res′ting-nes), ''n.'' The state or condition of being unresting; absence of repose or quiet. ''De Quincey'', Roman Meals.

'''unrestored''' (un-rē-stōrd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not restored; not given back.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then does he say he lent me
Some shipping ''unrestored.'' ''Shak.'', A. and C., iii. 6. 27.</poem>}}
'''2.''' Not restored to a former, and especially a better, state: as, ''unrestored'' health; ''unrestored'' to favor.
{{smaller block|If ''unrestor’d'' by this, despair your cure.
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, ii. 637.}}}}
'''3.''' In the ''fine arts'', remaining, as a work of art, in the condition in which its author left it, save for damage of time, from the elements, etc. Compare ''restoration'', 2.
{{smaller block|<poem>The Bucentaur lies rotting ''unrestored'',
Neglected garment of her widowhood!</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv. 11.}}}}

'''unrestrained''' (un-rẹ̄-strānd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not restrained; not controlled; not confined; not hindered; not limited.
{{smaller block|The banquet that followed was generous; . . . mirth ''unrestrained'', except by propriety.
{{right|''Lord Cockburn'', Life of Jeffrey.}}}}
'''2.''' Licentious; loose.
{{smaller block|<poem>They say he daily doth frequent
With ''unrestrained'' loose companions.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., v. 3. 7.}}}}

'''unrestrainedly''' (un-rẹ̄-strā′ned-li), ''adv.'' In an unrestrained manner; without restraint or limitation.

{{smaller block|Many grow old in an ''unresolvedness'' whether to embrace Christianity or not; and many continue unresolved as long as they live. {{right|''J. Edwards'', Works, IV. 339.}}}}

'''unresolving''' (un-rē-zol′ving), ''a.'' Not resolving; undetermined. ''Dryden.''

'''unrespect†''' (un-rē-spekt′), ''n.'' Disrespect; want of respect or reverence; disesteem. ''Bp. Hall.''

'''unrespectable''' (un-rẹ̄-spek′ta-bl), ''a.'' Not respectable; disreputable; dishonorable.

{{smaller block|He makes no distinction of respectable and ''unrespectable.'' {{right|''H. Bushnell'', Sermons for the New Life, p. 341.}}}}

'''unrespective†''' (un-rẹ̄-spek′tiv), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not regarding circumstances or conditions; devoid of respect or consideration; regardless; unthinking.

<poem>I will converse with iron-witted fools
And ''unrespective'' boys; none are for me
That look unto me with considerate eyes.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 2. 29.}}}}
<poem>O too, too rude hand
Of ''unrespective'' death!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Marston'', Antonio and Mellida, II., iv. 3.}}}}

'''2.''' Not respected; used at random; unheeded; common.

<poem>Nor the remainder viands
We do not throw in ''unrespective'' sieve,
Because we now are full.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 2. 71.}}}}

'''unrespited''' (un-res′pi-ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not respited. —'''2†.''' Admitting no pause or intermission. ''Milton'', P. L., ii. 185.

'''unresponsal†''' (un-rẹ̄-spon′sa̤l), ''a.'' Irresponsible.

{{smaller block|A tithe or a crop of hay or corn which are ready to be carried away by force by ''unresponsal'' men. {{right|''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, p. 106. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unresponsible''' (un-rẹ̄-spon′si-bl), ''a.'' Irresponsible.

{{smaller block|His ''unresponsable'' memory can make us no satisfaction. {{right|''Fuller'', Worthies, Essex, i. 370. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unresponsibleness''' (un-rẹ̄-spon′si-bl-nes), ''n.'' Irresponsibility. ''Bp. Gauden'', Hieraspistes, p. 349.

'''unresponsive''' (un-rẹ̄-spon′siv), ''a.'' Not responsive.

'''unresponsiveness''' (un-rẹ̄-spon′siv-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unresponsive.

'''unrest''' (un-rest′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''unreste'' (= MLG. ''unreste, unraste'' = G. dial. ''unrast''); < ''un-'' + ''rest''<sup>1</sup>.] Lack of rest or quietude, physical or mental.
{{smaller block|“Is this,” quod she, “the cause of youre ''unreste?''”
{{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 248.}}
<poem>That ''unrest'' which men miscall delight
Can touch him not and torture not again.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Adonais, xl.}}}}

'''unrest†''' (un-rest′), ''v. t.'' [ME. ''unresten''; < ''unrest'', ''n.''] To disturb; deprive of rest.
{{smaller block|<poem>Goode is hem to slee,
For thai the swarme ''unresteth'', so thai crie.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 155.}}}}

'''unrestful''' (un-rest′fůl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not restful or at rest; restless. ''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 961.—'''2.''' Not affording rest or promotive of rest.

'''unrestfulness''' (un-rest′fůl-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being unrestful; restlessness; disquietude.
{{smaller block|Whiche put the said Vortiger to great ''unrestfulnesse.''
{{right|''Fabyan'', Chronicle, lxxxii. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''unresting''' (un-res′ting), ''a.'' Not resting; continually in motion or action; restless. ''Daniel'', Civil Wars, i.

'''unrestingly''' (un-res′ting-li), ''adv.'' In an unresting manner; continuously; without rest.

'''unrestingness''' (un-res′ting-nes), ''n.'' The state or condition of being unresting; absence of repose or quiet. ''De Quincey'', Roman Meals.

'''unrestored''' (un-rē-stōrd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not restored; not given back.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then does he say he lent me
Some shipping ''unrestored.'' ''Shak.'', A. and C., iii. 6. 27.</poem>}}
'''2.''' Not restored to a former, and especially a better, state: as, ''unrestored'' health; ''unrestored'' to favor.
{{smaller block|If ''unrestor’d'' by this, despair your cure.
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, ii. 637.}}}}
'''3.''' In the ''fine arts'', remaining, as a work of art, in the condition in which its author left it, save for damage of time, from the elements, etc. Compare ''restoration'', 2.
{{smaller block|<poem>The Bucentaur lies rotting ''unrestored'',
Neglected garment of her widowhood!</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv. 11.}}}}

'''unrestrained''' (un-rẹ̄-strānd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not restrained; not controlled; not confined; not hindered; not limited.
{{smaller block|The banquet that followed was generous; . . . mirth ''unrestrained'', except by propriety.
{{right|''Lord Cockburn'', Life of Jeffrey.}}}}
'''2.''' Licentious; loose.
{{smaller block|<poem>They say he daily doth frequent
With ''unrestrained'' loose companions.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., v. 3. 7.}}}}

'''unrestrainedly''' (un-rẹ̄-strā′ned-li), ''adv.'' In an unrestrained manner; without restraint or limitation. {{smaller block|She . . . wept ''unrestrainedly''. {{right|''The Atlantic'', LXV. 541.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
